strengths: Addresses a genuine and important problem in joint speech-text modeling: the sequence-length mismatch between speech and text tokens, which is a recognized bottleneck for SLM quality.

The proposed cross-attention-based aggregation mechanism that leverages an ASR-initialized encoder-decoder to implicitly align speech representations to text token boundaries (without explicit forced alignment) is a reasonably elegant end-to-end solution.

TASTE achieves markedly lower bitrate/token-rate than baselines (SpeechTokenizer, S3 token) while retaining comparable or better reconstruction quality (WER, UTMOS) and similarity metrics, which is a compelling efficiency result.

Demonstrates that a full LLM can be adapted into a competent SLM using only LoRA fine-tuning, yielding accuracy comparable to prior full-finetuning approaches on SALMON and superior results on StoryCloze, supporting the claim that reducing modality mismatch alleviates catastrophic forgetting.

Evaluation covers multiple complementary aspects (acoustic quality, speaker/emotion/duration similarity, semantic coherence via StoryCloze, acoustic discrimination via SALMON), and includes both discrete token and continuous embedding modeling variants.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to CosyVoice's S3 tokenizer (which also derives tokens from ASR encoder shallow features); the paper's main addition is the aggregation/quantization scheme, which is not clearly disentangled or ablated against the CosyVoice baseline design choices.

No ablation studies are provided for key architectural decisions (e.g., choice of shallow layer for V, using last layer for K, number of RVQ layers/codebook size, aggregator depth), making it hard to assess which components actually drive the reported gains.

Table 2 comparisons mix models of different sizes, training regimes (LoRA vs. full fine-tuning), and training data, so claims of 'comparable performance' to full fine-tuning baselines are not fully controlled and somewhat overstated (e.g., Spirit LM Expr. outperforms TASTE on 3 of 4 SALMON dimensions).

The approach fundamentally requires the full text transcription (via ASR) to define token boundaries before speech tokenization, raising serious concerns about streaming/real-time applicability that are not discussed or addressed at all, despite the motivation being natural human-LLM interaction.

Duration consistency is notably weaker than other methods, and the explanation given is post-hoc rationalization without further empirical support (e.g., no analysis of failure cases or breakdown by utterance length/dynamics).
Experiments are limited to a single LLM (Llama-3.2-1B) and English-only data; no scaling experiments or multilingual evaluation, limiting the generality and significance of the claims.

Reproducibility is a concern: the pipeline depends on multiple external proprietary/pretrained components (Distil-Whisper, CosyVoice S3 tokens and vocoder), and no code/checkpoint release is mentioned.

The paper lacks human evaluation of generated speech quality/naturalness/expressiveness, relying solely on automatic metrics (UTMOS, WER, speaker similarity), which may not fully capture perceptual quality or paralinguistic preservation.
Writing has multiple typos, broken references (e.g., 'illustrate in Figure ,'), and inconsistent notation, which slightly hurts clarity and polish for a top-tier venue.

strengths: The core idea of aligning speech token sequence length to text token/word boundaries in an end-to-end, ASR-initialized manner (without requiring explicit forced alignment) is a reasonable and potentially useful direction for closing the speech-text modality gap.

The reconstruction evaluation shows TASTE achieves comparable quality/similarity to SpeechTokenizer at roughly 10x lower bitrate, and UTMOS scores are competitive, suggesting the aggregation+RVQ scheme is effective at compressing speech into a text-aligned representation.

Demonstrating that a 1B LLM adapted via LoRA with TASTE tokens/embeddings can approach the performance of full-finetuning baselines (TWIST, Spirit LM) on SALMON and StoryCloze is a meaningful efficiency claim if it holds up.

The paper explores two variants (discrete token modeling and continuous embedding modeling) and finds they perform similarly, which is a nice piece of evidence for the robustness of the underlying representation.
weaknesses: Critical methodological gap: the paper never clearly explains how the model performs autoregressive speech generation at inference time, since TASTE alignment/aggregation depends on having ASR text and word boundaries available. It is unclear whether generation is only evaluated via likelihood scoring on existing speech (as in SALMON/StoryCloze) or whether the model can actually synthesize novel speech token sequences on its own, and if so, how word/text boundaries are decided during free generation. No generated audio samples or generation examples are shown.

Comparisons in Table 2 are confounded: TASLM (1B, LoRA) is compared against much larger, fully fine-tuned prior models (TWIST 1.3B, Spirit LM, pGSLM) trained on different data/architectures. Claims of 'comparable performance despite reduced parameters' are not well isolated from differences in base model, training data scale, and training paradigm, making it hard to attribute gains specifically to TASTE.

No ablation studies are provided for key architectural choices: the choice of shallow layer k, the necessity of using both h_last and h_shallow in the aggregator, the number of RVQ layers/codebook size, or the importance of ASR-based initialization versus random initialization. These are central design decisions left unvalidated.

The duration-consistency metric is notably weaker than baselines (0.73 vs 0.82–0.88 for SpeechTokenizer, and 0.83 for the S3 topline), which is dismissed somewhat casually in the text as an inherent consequence of dynamic compression, but this is a significant limitation for a tokenization method aimed at preserving paralinguistic information.

The vocoder and target speech units (S3 tokens, flow-matching + HiFiGAN) are borrowed wholesale from CosyVoice and frozen, so the 'reconstruction quality' is substantially bounded by an external, non-trained component; this limits the novelty and end-to-end nature of the claimed contribution.

Evaluation relies entirely on automatic metrics (WER, UTMOS, speaker/emotion classifiers, likelihood-based benchmark accuracy) with no human listening study or qualitative analysis of generated speech naturalness/coherence, which is a significant gap for a paper about spoken language generation.

The 'Baseline (S3 token)' comparison in Table 2 performs remarkably poorly (near chance on SALMON), which raises questions about whether the baseline was fairly tuned/trained under the same LoRA budget and epochs as TASLM, since such a large gap versus TASTE seems disproportionate and is not sufficiently analyzed.

On StoryCloze, TASLM still lags substantially behind the ASR+LLM cascade topline (64.2/88.9 vs 73.5/95.9), indicating that the claimed mitigation of catastrophic forgetting/modality mismatch is only partial, yet the paper's framing suggests a stronger success story than the numbers support.

The experimental scale (1B model, ~40k+600 hours of training data) is modest relative to contemporary SLM literature (Moshi, Spirit LM use larger scale), and it is unclear whether the proposed alignment mechanism would scale gracefully to larger models/datasets.

The writing contains numerous grammatical errors and typos (e.g., 'recent progress have focused', 'genearate', 'druing', 'Consine' scheduler, 'sopken', 'stemmed from the two key observations'), and some figure/equation references are broken or unclear (e.g., 'illustrate in Figure ,' missing figure number), reducing overall polish and clarity.
No statistical significance testing or variance reporting (e.g., across seeds) is provided for the benchmark results, which is important given the fairly small differences between methods in Table 2.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and important problem in spoken language modeling: the length/modality mismatch between speech and text tokens, which is a recognized bottleneck for joint speech-text SLMs.

The core technical idea—aligning speech tokenization length with text transcription length via a novel cross-attention aggregation mechanism (using shallow encoder representations as values) combined with ASR-model initialization—is a genuinely novel, end-to-end approach that requires no explicit forced alignment.

Strong empirical results on speech reconstruction: TASTE achieves reconstruction quality (UTMOS, WER, speaker/emotion similarity) comparable to or better than baselines while using an order of magnitude lower bitrate, demonstrating the tokenization retains rich paralinguistic information despite aggressive compression.

Practical significance: by resolving the length mismatch, the paper shows text LLMs can be adapted into competent SLMs using only LoRA fine-tuning rather than full fine-tuning, which is an appealing efficiency argument for the field.

Reasonably comprehensive downstream evaluation across two established benchmarks (SALMON for acoustic properties, StoryCloze for semantic coherence) and against several strong prior SLMs (TWIST, pGSLM, Spirit LM).
Exploration of two modeling variants (discrete token vs. continuous embedding prediction) shows the representation is robust and generalizes across modeling paradigms, adding methodological interest.
The paper is mostly clearly organized, with figures illustrating the pipeline that aid understanding of a fairly complex multi-stage system.
weaknesses: No ablation studies are provided for key design choices (e.g., choice of shallow vs. last hidden layer for K/V in the aggregator, RVQ layer count, initialization strategy, effect of word-level averaging/grouping on final performance), making it hard to assess which components drive the gains.

The efficiency/compute benefits of reduced token length are claimed repeatedly but never empirically substantiated with concrete inference latency, throughput, or training-time comparisons against baselines.

Duration consistency, one of the similarity metrics, shows a larger gap versus toplines than other metrics, and this weakness is somewhat downplayed rather than analyzed in depth (e.g., no error analysis of where/why duration modeling fails).
The gap to the ASR+LLM topline on StoryCloze remains sizable (e.g., 88.9/89.5 vs 95.9 on tSC), and the paper does not thoroughly discuss what limits further closing this gap.

Evaluation relies entirely on automatic metrics (WER, UTMOS, embedding-based similarity/consistency); there is no human evaluation of speech naturalness/quality or of SLM continuation outputs, which is standard practice for TTS/SLM papers and would strengthen claims about paralinguistic fidelity.

The method has a strong dependency on ASR transcription quality, but there is no analysis of robustness to ASR errors or noisy/low-resource conditions, despite this being central to the tokenizer's construction.

Experiments are limited to a single LLM backbone (Llama-3.2-1B) and a single language (English), so scalability to larger models and multilingual settings is untested, despite the training data (Emilia) being multilingual.
The vocabulary mismatch resolution (word-level grouping/averaging/alignment in Algorithm 1) is a fairly ad hoc post-processing step with no quantitative assessment of information loss it introduces.
Minor writing/typo issues throughout (e.g., "langauge," "sopken," "Consine," "traning," "Whipser") suggest the manuscript would benefit from a careful proofreading pass.

Comparisons in Table 2 mix models of different sizes and full fine-tuning vs. LoRA, and while this is acknowledged, a more controlled comparison (e.g., LoRA baseline with S3 tokens at matched LLM size) beyond the single S3 baseline row would better isolate the contribution of text alignment itself versus other confounds.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea: aligning speech tokens with text transcription tokens directly at the tokenization stage via a cross-attention aggregator, addressing the length-mismatch problem that plagues joint speech-text modeling, rather than relying on heuristic interleaving or padding used in prior work.

Achieves extremely low bitrate (~150bps) while maintaining reconstruction quality (UTMOS/DNSMOS) that rivals or exceeds ground truth, and reasonably competitive similarity metrics compared to codecs operating at much higher bitrates.

Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation: reconstruction quality/similarity (objective + MUSHRA human test), qualitative text-aligned speech editing demonstration, speech continuation (GPT-4o, UTMOS, human MOS), likelihood-based benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze), and few-shot spoken QA.

Strong empirical results in speech continuation: a 1.3B-parameter model fine-tuned with lightweight LoRA outperforms much larger (7B) pretrained SLMs across all continuation metrics, and is the only SLM shown not to degrade the underlying text LLM's capability.
Ablation against a baseline using S3 tokens directly for joint modeling (without text-alignment) clearly shows the benefit of the proposed alignment mechanism.

Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed training hyperparameters, evaluation protocols/instructions, and an explicit algorithm for handling ASR/LLM vocabulary mismatch are provided in the appendix.
Provides two modeling variants (discrete token-based and continuous embedding-based) demonstrating that the underlying TASTE representation is flexible.
weaknesses: The approach fundamentally depends on having an ASR transcription available both during training and inference to derive/query the tokenizer, which somewhat undercuts the 'speech-only tokenization' framing and raises questions about real-world streaming applicability (acknowledged only briefly as future work).

Comparisons in Table 2 are not fully controlled: TASLM uses only ~45M LoRA parameters atop a 1.3B model trained on a much larger pretraining corpus (40k hours Emilia) versus baselines with different data scale/model size, making it hard to isolate whether gains come from TASTE itself or from data/backbone advantages.

No ablation study justifying key architectural choices in the aggregator (e.g., using last-layer hidden state as key and shallow-layer as value); the justification is intuitive/qualitative rather than empirically validated with alternative designs.

Duration consistency is second-worst among all compared tokenization methods, suggesting the dynamic, text-aligned compression sacrifices some fine-grained temporal/paralinguistic fidelity, which is a core claimed strength of the method.

Human evaluation sample sizes are relatively small (20 samples per method), and the paper does not report inter-rater reliability or more rigorous statistical significance testing beyond confidence intervals.

Missing direct comparison with more recent end-to-end joint speech-text systems (e.g., Moshi, Mini-Omni) on the speech continuation benchmark, limiting the ability to contextualize TASLM's gains against the most competitive joint-modeling baselines.
Evaluation restricted to English only; multilingual generalizability is unverified.

The paper does not discuss computational overhead or latency introduced by the ASR + cross-attention aggregation stage compared to simpler codec-based tokenizers, which is relevant for practical deployment claims.

strengths: The core idea—aligning speech tokens to text transcription tokens via a cross-attention aggregator at the tokenization stage—is a clean, well-motivated solution to the classic speech-text length-mismatch problem in joint spoken language modeling, avoiding heuristic padding or interleaving used by prior work.

Extremely low bitrate (~150 bps) reconstruction while achieving competitive or superior quality metrics (UTMOS, DNSMOS) compared to codecs operating at several times higher bitrate is a notable empirical result.

The text-aligned speech editing experiment (word-level token swapping) is a nice qualitative demonstration that the tokenization genuinely captures word-level paralinguistic information (e.g., duration).

Reasonably broad evaluation suite: reconstruction (objective + MUSHRA), speech continuation (GPT-4o, UTMOS, human MOS), likelihood-based benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze), and spoken QA, going beyond a single metric.

The method enables parameter-efficient adaptation (LoRA) of an off-the-shelf text LLM into a competitive SLM with far fewer trainable/base parameters (1.3B) than several baselines (7B), suggesting practical efficiency benefits if the comparisons are fair.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons in Table 2 mix models of very different scale and training data (1.3B TASLM vs 7B TWIST/Spirit LM, trained on different corpora), making it hard to attribute gains specifically to TASTE tokenization rather than differences in base LLM, training data scale (40k hrs Emilia), or LoRA fine-tuning recipe; no controlled ablation isolates the tokenization's contribution from these confounds.

Duration consistency, one of the paper's central paralinguistic-preservation claims, is actually the second-worst among all compared methods in Table 1, undercutting the narrative that TASTE 'preserves essential paralinguistic information' relative to fixed-rate tokenizers.

No ablations are provided for key architectural choices: why last-hidden-state as key vs. shallow as value, sensitivity to the choice of shallow layer l, RVQ depth R=4, codebook size, or the aggregator's number of attention layers—these design choices are asserted via intuition rather than empirically justified.
Human evaluation is based on only 20 samples per method, which is a small sample size for drawing statistically robust conclusions, especially given the large reported standard deviations.

The paper does not address latency/streaming feasibility in any experiment, despite requiring full ASR transcription and word-level alignment before tokenization; this is acknowledged only as a limitation without any empirical or architectural analysis of the real-world cost.

Spoken QA comparisons (Table 3) pit a pretrained-only TASLM against fully instruction-tuned models (Moshi, Llama-Omni, Mini-Omni), which is an unfair comparison in favor of the paper's claims about 'not degrading' the base LLM, since instruction-tuned baselines are optimized for a different objective entirely.

The claimed novelty over CosyVoice's S3 tokenizer (which also uses text-conditioned representations) is only lightly differentiated; the technical distinction from prior text-speech cross-attention work (e.g., Chen & Rudnicky) is argued rather than empirically demonstrated.

Only English data is evaluated, and no analysis is given on ASR transcription error sensitivity (WER of the ASR model propagating into tokenization quality), which is a core dependency of the entire method.

The word-level vocabulary alignment procedure (Appendix A.2) is fairly complex and heuristic (grouping/averaging/duplicating based on word boundaries from two different tokenizers), yet its impact on quality/robustness is not separately evaluated.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach: aligning speech tokens with text transcription tokens directly at the tokenization stage via a cross-attention aggregator, addressing the length-mismatch problem that plagues prior joint speech-text modeling approaches without requiring explicit alignment or heuristic padding/interleaving.

End-to-end trainable pipeline using only a reconstruction objective to learn text-aligned discrete speech tokens/embeddings, which is a clean and elegant design compared to prior multi-stage alignment techniques.

Strong empirical results on speech reconstruction: TASTE achieves very low bitrate (~150 bps) while attaining competitive or superior quality scores (UTMOS/DNSMOS even exceeding ground truth) and near-topline MUSHRA scores.
Demonstrates an interesting downstream capability (text-aligned speech editing) that showcases the interpretability and controllability benefits of the text-aligned tokenization.

Comprehensive evaluation of spoken language modeling combining objective metrics (UTMOS, likelihood-based SALMON/StoryCloze), LLM-based scoring (GPT-4o), and human listening tests, adding robustness to the claims.
Impressive parameter efficiency: a 1.3B TASLM with LoRA fine-tuning outperforms much larger (7B) pretrained SLMs on speech continuation tasks across nearly all evaluated metrics.
Includes a meaningful ablation (Baseline with S3 token for joint modeling) that isolates the contribution of TASTE's text-alignment property, supporting the core claim.
Good transparency: detailed appendix with training hyperparameters, human evaluation protocols/instructions, GPT-4o prompt templates, and reported standard deviations for all tables.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to English only; the applicability and effectiveness of ASR-transcription-dependent tokenization for other languages, especially morphologically rich or low-resource ones, is untested and could reveal significant challenges.

The approach fundamentally depends on ASR transcription quality; the paper does not analyze robustness to or propagation of ASR errors, which could meaningfully degrade tokenization and downstream modeling performance in noisier or more diverse domains than LibriSpeech/LibriTTS.

Duration consistency and ViSQOL scores are among the weakest across compared tokenizers (second-worst or below several fixed-rate codecs), which somewhat undercuts the framing that TASTE achieves comprehensively superior reconstruction quality at low bitrate.

SALMON/StoryCloze results are only 'comparable' (not clearly superior) to prior 7B models, so the headline claim of outperforming other SLMs is strongest mainly for the continuation task rather than uniformly across all benchmarks.

The comparison in the spoken QA experiment (Table 3) pits a pretrained-only model using few-shot prompting against instruction-tuned models (Moshi, Llama-Omni), which is a somewhat uneven comparison, weakening the strength of the associated claims about understanding capability.

The novelty of the cross-attention aggregation mechanism itself is incremental relative to prior text-speech cross-attention work in TTS style transfer (acknowledged in the appendix); the core contribution is more about the framing/application (tokenization for joint LM) than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Word-level grouping/alignment procedure to reconcile ASR and LLM vocabularies (Appendix A.2) is somewhat ad hoc engineering that adds complexity and potential failure points (e.g., tokenization mismatches for rare words or non-Latin scripts) not deeply analyzed.

No analysis of computational overhead/latency introduced by requiring an ASR pass plus cross-attention aggregation compared to simpler single-pass speech tokenizers, despite the paper explicitly noting non-streaming/latency as a limitation without quantifying it.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and timely problem: the text-speech length mismatch and semantic redundancy in speech tokens for joint text-speech spoken language modeling.

The proposed attention-based aggregator (cross-attention using ASR encoder last hidden states as query-key source and shallow hidden states as values) is a clean, reasonably well-justified design choice, supported by CCA analysis (Fig. 6) and ablations (Table 4) that validate the use of shallow representations.

Extensive empirical evaluation: speech reconstruction quality/similarity (Table 1), speech continuation and likelihood-based benchmarks (Table 2, SALMON/StoryCloze), spoken QA preserving base LLM text performance (Table 3), tokenizer ablations (Table 4), and multiple robustness studies (ASR dependency, noise robustness, alternate ASR backbone) in the appendix.

TASTE achieves strong reconstruction quality at an extremely low bitrate (~150bps) compared to much higher-bitrate baselines, and downstream spoken LMs built on TASTE with only LoRA fine-tuning of a 1.3B model outperform larger (7B) pretrained SLMs on several human/automatic evaluations.
Interesting qualitative demonstration of text-aligned speech editing (paralinguistic transfer via token swapping) and few-shot spoken QA capability that other baselines lack.

Good transparency: reports standard deviations, ablations on ASR choice/quality, noise robustness, and discusses limitations candidly (single-speaker, English-only, no non-lexical events, latency/streaming unaddressed).
Demo/code/models promised for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core novelty (text-speech cross-attention for aggregation) is explicitly acknowledged by the authors as related to prior content-style cross-attention mechanisms in TTS (Chen & Rudnicky, 2022); the technical contribution is somewhat incremental, combining known components (cross-attention aggregation, RVQ, LoRA, MELLE-style latent modeling) rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques.

The tokenization scheme fundamentally requires (pseudo-)text transcription alignment, which is at odds with a truly generative/flexible SLM: the token stream is by construction locked to word boundaries, limiting the ability to represent non-lexical or overlapping/multi-speaker phenomena (acknowledged as a limitation but is a substantial scope restriction).

Comparisons in the main continuation/likelihood table (Table 2) are against relatively dated or smaller/moderate baselines (TWIST, Spirit LM); no direct quantitative comparison to more recent strong hybrid text-speech systems mentioned in related work (e.g., Moshi, Mini-Omni) on the same continuation/likelihood benchmarks, despite these being discussed as the 'prevailing paradigm.'

Evaluation relies heavily on GPT-4o as a semantic judge and MUSHRA/MOS via crowdsourced (MTurk) listeners, which can introduce subjectivity/bias; only 20 samples with ~10 raters are used for human evaluations, which is a fairly small sample size for statistical robustness.

The method is only evaluated on English (LibriSpeech, Emilia English subset, LibriTTS); generalization to other languages, accents, or more spontaneous/noisy real-world speech (beyond the synthetic noise robustness test) is unverified.

The overall system involves considerable engineering complexity (ASR frontend, encoder-aggregator-quantizer pipeline, word-level grouping/averaging/alignment algorithm to reconcile ASR/LLM vocabulary mismatch in Appendix A.4, weighted-sum fusion), which is somewhat at odds with the claimed 'simplicity' and 'no explicit alignment' framing, since a full word-level alignment procedure is still required in practice.

SALMON results show TASLM notably underperforms on background/room/environmental attributes, indicating the tokenizer's paralinguistic modeling is narrowly tuned to clean, single-speaker natural speech and doesn't generalize to broader acoustic scene information.

strengths: The core idea—deriving speech tokens via cross-attention that queries on the text transcription so that speech tokens are length-aligned one-to-one with text tokens—is a clean and well-motivated solution to the text/speech sequence-length mismatch problem that plagues joint text-speech LM decoding.

The tokenizer achieves an extremely low bitrate (~150 bps, ~3 tokens/sec) while remaining competitive with or superior to much higher-bitrate codecs (SpeechTokenizer, Mimi, Encodec) in WER, UTMOS/DNSMOS, and MUSHRA, supporting the claim that paralinguistic rather than lexical content is being encoded.

Evaluation is broad: reconstruction quality/similarity (Table 1), speech continuation with GPT-4o/UTMOS/human MOS and likelihood-based benchmarks (SALMON, StoryCloze), spoken QA under few-shot, plus a qualitative text-aligned speech-editing demonstration.

Multiple thoughtful ablations are provided: module-wise ablation of encoder/aggregator/quantizer, choice of shallow vs. last hidden layer justified via CCA analysis, sensitivity to ASR errors and to using a different ASR backbone, and robustness under additive noise at multiple SNRs — these substantially strengthen the soundness of the design choices.

The result that a 1.3B model fine-tuned only with LoRA on TASTE outperforms much larger (7B) pretrained SLMs on continuation quality, while an S3-token joint model trained the same way performs far worse, is a fairly convincing piece of evidence that the tokenization design (not just model scale) matters for joint modeling.

The paper is clearly written, includes detailed appendices (training details, human-eval instructions, algorithm for handling ASR/LLM vocabulary mismatch), and reports standard deviations, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The main continuation comparison (Table 2) pits a 1.3B TASLM against 7B baselines (TWIST 7B, Spirit LM Expressive), which is an unfair/uncontrolled comparison in the opposite direction of typical scaling expectations; a same-scale comparison (1.3B vs 1.3B) is present but limited, and no comparison to more recent strong joint tokenizers (e.g., Moshi/Mimi, GLM-4-Voice) is included as an SLM baseline despite Mimi being used in the tokenizer-only comparison.

The method is not fully end-to-end as advertised: it depends on a frozen, pretrained Whisper ASR encoder for both tokenization and for the target unit-to-speech vocoder/flow model taken from prior work (Du et al., 2024a), so error propagation and dependency on external, non-jointly-trained components remain a practical limitation, even though the ASR-noise ablation suggests the effect is currently small on clean-ish data.

Evaluation is restricted to English, single-speaker, relatively clean read/in-the-wild speech (LibriSpeech/LibriTTS/Emilia); the paper explicitly lists lack of multilingual, multi-speaker, and non-lexical-event handling as limitations, so generalizability of the claimed benefits is unverified.

The text-aligned speech editing capability, one of the paper's highlighted contributions, is demonstrated only qualitatively (a single example pair and spectrogram visualization) with no quantitative evaluation (e.g., editing success rate, perceptual study), making it hard to assess robustness of this claimed capability.

Human evaluation sample sizes are modest (20 samples per method with MTurk raters), which limits statistical confidence in the human MOS/MUSHRA comparisons, and details on rater quality control/inter-rater agreement are not reported.

Claims of novelty ('first end-to-end approach... tailored for text-speech spoken language modeling') are somewhat strong given that concurrent/prior work (Xie & Wu 2024a, Zeng et al. 2024, Du et al. 2024a) already pursue reducing token frequency or text-speech alignment for joint modeling; the differentiation is argued but not empirically compared head-to-head against these closely related reduction/alignment strategies under matched settings.

The likelihood-based SALMON results show TASLM notably underperforming on background/room/domain acoustic-consistency subtasks, indicating the tokenizer's paralinguistic coverage is narrower than claimed (limited largely to speaker/gender/prosody), which somewhat undercuts the general 'preserves essential paralinguistic information' framing in the abstract.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach: TASTE directly tackles the length-mismatch problem between text and speech tokens by aligning speech tokens one-to-one with text tokens at the tokenization stage, via an attention-based aggregator, rather than relying on post-hoc heuristics like interleaving, padding, or delayed decoding used in prior work.

Strong empirical results across multiple axes: speech reconstruction quality/similarity comparable to much higher-bitrate codecs despite operating at ~150 bps and ~3 tokens/sec; substantial improvements in speech continuation (GPT-4o, UTMOS, human MOS) over strong baselines (TWIST, Spirit LM) at smaller parameter counts and with only LoRA fine-tuning; competitive likelihood-based evaluation on SALMON/StoryCloze.

Thorough ablations and robustness checks: module-wise ablation of encoder/aggregator/quantizer, ASR-dependence ablation (ASR vs ground-truth transcription, alternate ASR model), noise robustness study across SNR levels, and layer selection justified via CCA analysis, which together substantiate the design choices.

Demonstrates versatility beyond the core contribution: text-aligned speech editing (swapping paralinguistic content while preserving words) and few-shot spoken QA capability that preserves the base text LLM's performance, unlike other joint SLMs which degrade substantially when adding speech modality.

Good transparency and reproducibility efforts: detailed appendices covering training hyperparameters, evaluation protocols (MUSHRA, MOS instructions, GPT-4o prompt), algorithm for handling ASR/LLM vocabulary mismatch, and disclosure of LLM usage for writing assistance.
Clear writing and figures that effectively communicate the concept (Figure 1) and architecture (Figure 2), aiding understanding of a fairly intricate pipeline.
weaknesses: The approach fundamentally depends on ASR quality to obtain the text transcription used for alignment; although ablations show robustness to ASR errors on clean LibriSpeech/Emilia data, this reliance could be more consequential in more challenging domains (heavy accents, code-switching, overlapping speech) which are not tested.

Evaluation is restricted to English and largely single-speaker, read/clean speech (LibriSpeech, LibriTTS, Emilia-English); generalization to other languages, spontaneous conversational speech, multi-speaker or noisy real-world scenarios is only discussed as future work, not empirically verified.

The method explicitly cannot represent non-lexical or paralinguistic content that lacks textual correspondence (e.g., laughter, overlapping speech, non-speech sounds), which is acknowledged as a limitation but somewhat limits claims of general-purpose spoken tokenization.

The word-level alignment/averaging procedure (Algorithm 1) needed to reconcile ASR and LLM vocabulary mismatch adds complexity and potential information loss (via averaging within word groups) that is not deeply analyzed for its own effect on final performance.

Comparisons in Table 2/3 mix model scales and base LLMs in some cases (e.g., different base parameter counts, LoRA vs full fine-tuning) which, while explained, somewhat complicates strictly fair apples-to-apples comparisons across all baselines.

The paper relies on a frozen pre-trained Whisper encoder and existing S3 tokenizer/vocoder components from Du et al., so part of the pipeline is not fully novel; the core novelty is concentrated in the aggregator/alignment mechanism and training objective.
